sentences.text: The name Coronosaurus combines Latin and Greek roots for 'crown' and 'lizard', honoring the crown-like plates on its skull that inspired the name.
This dinosaur featured a large frill, brow horns, a nasal horn, and unique irregular spiky bone masses that formed from short spines fusing together as the animal grew.
Adults had inflated brow horns that did not extend sideways over the eye sockets, unlike the long side-projections seen in some other horned dinosaurs.
Gregory S. Paul estimated in 2010 that the creature reached a length of 5 meters and a mass of 2 tonnes.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is cataloged as TMP 2002.68.1 and consists of a large adult-sized parietal bone with an almost complete midline bar.
Coronosaurus possesses a unique epiparietal 3 that develops variably as a short tongue-shaped hook or a conical tip oriented dorsolaterally.
Phillip J. Currie discovered the remains in two bone beds within the Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada, between 1996 and 2000.
Most, if not all, of the ceratopsian material from bone bed BB 138 in Dinosaur Provincial Park and the MRR BB near Warner has been referred to this species.
Studies suggest that the environment where Coronosaurus lived was an ancient coastal plain.
The Oldman Formation also contains remains of various theropods, ceratopsids, hadrosaurids, and ankylosaurids.
Michael J. Ryan and Anthony P. Russell originally described the type species as Centrosaurus brinkmani in 2005, but Ryan, Evans, and Shepherd established the separate genus Coronosaurus in 2012.
The animal is classified in the class Ornithischia, the family Ceratopsidae, the subfamily Centrosaurinae, and the subgroup Centrosaurini.

Phylogenetic analysis identified Coronosaurus as the sister taxon to Styracosaurus, placing it in a more advanced position than Centrosaurus apertus, though later studies placed it as a sister taxon to a clade formed by Centrosaurus and Spinops.
Coronosaurus lived during the middle Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, a time range spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
In 2016, Ryan et al. placed Coronosaurus as a sister taxon to a clade formed by Centrosaurus and Spinops, separate from Styracosaurus and Rubeosaurus, all within Centrosaurini.
